Q: Angular 19 returning partially correct DTOs from server eventhough all server data is correct A:

I bet the SurveyDto and TripApplicationDtos will also always be null on the client side. I can't tell from your example since their input is already null.

You will need to provide mappings for all your classes used inside your structure. You have only provided mappings for Article and Trip. You will need to add mappings also for TripTerm, TripApplication and Survey. Classes like List and ICollection should work out of the box, since their mappings are already provided by .NET.

If the class doesn't contain any other of your classes, the mapping can be as simple as:

CreateMap<TripTerm, TripTermDTO>().ReverseMap();

Q: Trying to switch between images with a single button using JavaScript A:

You're making an assumption here:

if (current__img.src != image1)

When debugging this comparison, observe the actual value of current__img.src. You'll likely find that the browser has modified it to a full URL, not just the relative URL you're using. As a result, the two values in this comparison will never be equal.

Instead, check if the src value simply ends with your relative URL value:

if (current__img.src.endsWith(image1))

Q: How to pass important page data without losing it on reload? A:

hello Karthick Raja **
Web architecture requires the URL to be the "source of truth."** In Flutter Web, the extra parameter is stored in the browser's history state, but it is notorious for being unreliable or cleared on hard reloads depending on the browser.

The production-grade pattern is the "ID + Cache" approach.

The Strategy: URL ID with extra Optimization

Instead of choosing between the URL and extra, use both.

  1. The URL contains the ID: This ensures the page is bookmarkable and survives a reload.

  2. The extra contains the Object: This acts as a "fast-track" so mobile and internal web navigation don't need to re-fetch data.

  3. The Repository handles the logic: If extra is null (on reload), the repository fetches the data using the ID from the URL.

Code Implementation Example

Dart

// 1. Define the route with a Path Parameter
GoRoute(
  path: '/details/:id',
  name: 'details',
  builder: (context, state) {
    final id = state.pathParameters['id']!;
    // Try to get the object from 'extra'
    final object = state.extra as MyObject?; 

    return DetailsPage(
      id: id,
      preLoadedObject: object, // Pass it as an optional optimization
    );
  },
),

// 2. Navigation
context.goNamed(
  'details', 
  pathParameters: {'id': myObject.id}, 
  extra: myObject, // Passed for instant UI on mobile/web-internal nav
);

How to handle the "Reload" in the Widget

In your DetailsPage (or your ViewModel/Bloc), use a FutureBuilder or equivalent:

  • If preLoadedObject is NOT null: Show the UI immediately.

  • If preLoadedObject IS null (Reload case): Use the id to fetch the data from your local cache (like a Map in a Singleton) or your API.

Why this is "Production-Grade":

  • Mobile Performance: On mobile, you almost never trigger a "reload," so extra is always there. No redundant API calls.

  • Web Durability: If a user hits F5, the app restarts, sees the :id in the URL, and fetches the necessary data.

  • Security/Size: You aren't stuffing a huge JSON string into the URL; you're only putting a standard resource identifier.

[!TIP] If the data is extremely sensitive and shouldn't be in the API/Database, you can use sessionStorage (via the dart:html or package:web library) as a middle-ground. Unlike localStorage, sessionStorage is wiped when the tab is closed, but survives a page reload.

Q: How to hide a password send to a web API from Windows logging A:

In essence, it is generally a bad practice to script password authentication simply because you can't trust a script. You need to lay the trust in the hands of a user (account) or an organization.
From a technically view, a SecureString is reasonable safe, but putting a plain-text secret in it or getting a plain-text secret out of it is not. So what is the use of a SecureString? Almost nothing, other than just passing it through from an entity you do trust to another entity you do trust, like this:

$Credential = Get-Credential
Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post -Uri $Uri -Credential $Credential #...

Where you might conclude that a SecureString shouldn't be used at all and simply rely on the permissions of the current user (or computer) account:

⚠️ Recommendation

Don't use SecureString for new code. When porting code to .NET Core, consider that the contents of the array are not encrypted in memory. The general approach of dealing with credentials is to avoid them and instead rely on other means to authenticate, such as certificates or Windows authentication.

Anyways, if your company doesn't leave you any other option, you might leverage from the feature that the -body parameter accepts either a (json) string or a hash table (dictionary):

When the input is a POST request and the body is a String, the value to the left of the first equals sign (=) is set as a key in the form data and the remaining text is set as the value. To specify multiple keys, use an IDictionary object, such as a hash table, for the Body.

Meaning : do not use a Json-string but use a HashTable instead (knowing that a HashTable is stringified to System.Collections.Hashtable in the output):

$Body = @{
    username          = $Credential.UserName
    password          = $Credential.Password | ConvertFrom-SecureString -AsPlainText
    concurrentSession = $true
} # Don't use: | ConvertTo-Json

Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post -Uri $Uri -Body $Body -TimeoutSec 2700 # Don't use: -ContentType "application/json"

Windows log:

Again, this is just a workaround called "Security through obscurity". I can't guaranty that your plain-test password might end up anywhere else once retrieved from something like a SecureString!

Q: How do 'cluster' and 'worker_threads' work in Node.js? A:

Effectively what you are differing is process based vs thread based. Threads share memory (e.g. SharedArrayBuffer) whereas processes don't. Essentially they are the same thing categorically.

cluster

  • One process is launched on each CPU and can communicate via IPC.
  • Each process has it's own memory with it's own Node (v8) instance. Creating tons of them may create memory issues.
  • Great for spawning many HTTP servers that share the same port b/c the main process will multiplex the requests to the child processes.

worker threads

  • One process total

  • Creates multiple threads with each thread having one Node instance (one event loop, one JS engine). Most Node API's are available to each thread except a few. So essentially Node is embedding itself and creating a new thread.

  • Shares memory with other threads (e.g. SharedArrayBuffer)

  • Great for CPU intensive tasks like processing data or accessing the file system. Because NodeJS is single threaded, synchronous tasks can be made more efficient with workers

Q: AWS Lambda cannot POST json without application/json header in the Request A:

You can’t add Content-Type headers inside Lambda. Headers must be sent by the client or API Gateway. Your issue happens because when you test in the Lambda console, you’re not sending an API Gateway–formatted event, so request.getBody() becomes null.

Why Postman works but Lambda console test fails

  • Postman → API Gateway → Lambda

    API Gateway builds a proper APIGatewayProxyRequestEvent with body and headers.

  • Lambda console “Test”

    Sends raw JSON, not an API Gateway event → request.getBody() is null.

How to test correctly in console

Use an API Gateway proxy event JSON, like:

{
  "body": "{\"id\":1,\"itemName\":\"Pen\",\"quantity\":3}",
  "headers": { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
  "httpMethod": "POST",
  "path": "/order",
  "isBase64Encoded": false
}

In real usage

Just make sure your client sends:

Content-Type: application/json

Lambda itself cannot add this header for incoming requests.

So: nothing is wrong with your Lambda code — it’s only the way you’re testing from the console.
